claims.text: The starting material is a coarse-grained, as-cast or standard powder-processed refractory high-entropy alloy with limited prior thermomechanical treatment.
The proposed intervention combines cold or warm rolling, intercritical annealing, and controlled recrystallization.
Multi-stage thermomechanical processing will refine and stabilize grains and subgrain-boundary networks in RHEAs.
The proposed benefit should hold above 1000 °C under high neutron flux or heavy-ion-plus-helium irradiation.
Dense grain and subgrain boundaries act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Dense grain and subgrain boundaries act as sinks for radiation-induced defects.
Impeded dislocation motion from the hierarchical microstructure enhances strength.
Abundant interfaces recombine and annihilate irradiation-induced defects.
The hierarchical interface network improves irradiation tolerance by reducing defect accumulation.
The hierarchical microstructure improves thermal stability.
The intervention will increase yield strength by 25–50% relative to coarse-grained RHEAs at service temperatures above 1000 °C.
The refined material will maintain or improve microstructural stability under irradiation.
The appropriate baseline is a conventional coarse-grained RHEA produced by standard casting or powder metallurgy without additional refinement.
Performance gains depend on retaining fine, stable grains and boundaries at high temperature and under irradiation.
Excessive grain growth or boundary instability may degrade the proposed performance gains.
Heavy-ion-plus-helium irradiation at 1100 °C can simulate relevant reactor exposure conditions for the comparison.
The hierarchical material should accumulate fewer irradiation-induced voids, dislocation loops, or helium bubbles than the coarse-grained baseline.
Failure to achieve either the specified 25–50% strength improvement or reduced defect accumulation would falsify the hypothesis.
